responseNone: No system flow covers this alert
askExplain: Explain this attack and tell me what to do next
askAttacker: What else did this attacker do?
replayTip: Play every alert of this window in order
liveTip: Follow new alerts as they arrive
capBrute1: {{attempts}} failed sign-ins in {{minutes}} minutes, rotating {{count}} account names.
capBrute2: A sign-in for {{account}} succeeds right after the failures: the password was guessed.
capBrute3: Correlation of the failures across sources: one attacker, many accounts.
capOut4: The connection was dropped, and the alert was raised so the machine gets checked.
capOut5: The connection repeats: {{name}} is likely infected. Isolate it and find the process.
capLat0: {{name}}{{user}} reaches out to {{to}} inside the network.
capLatHowKerb: Kerberos service tickets it can crack offline
capLatHowAsrep: a Kerberos reply for an account without pre-authentication
capLat2: {{to}} accepts the session: the attacker now moves between machines.
capWeb2: {{perimeter}} recognizes the attack signatures and drops the requests.
capWeb2b: The IPS recognizes the attack signatures and drops the requests.
capWeb3: Some requests reach {{to}}; the server answers with errors and one 200 OK.
capWeb4: Block {{name}} and check the server's logs.
capTrv1: {{gap}} minutes later the same account signs in from {{city}}, {{country}}.
capTrv2: {{km}} km in {{gap}} minutes: no one travels that fast. The password is likely stolen.
capTrv3: Revoke the sessions and reset {{user}}'s password.
capScn0: {{name}} starts knocking on {{to}}, one port after another.
capScn1: {{count}} ports probed in seconds: SSH, SMB, RDP, databases, web consoles…
capScn2: Ports {{open}} answer; everything else is closed or filtered.
capScn3: Usually the first step of an attack: block the source.
capCl3: Confirm it was planned, or undo it.
capBlocked: {{ip}} is now blocked on {{on}}: the traffic stops here.
dLsass: dumps LSASS memory to steal passwords
dMiner: mines cryptocurrency with the server CPU
dRev: opens an interactive shell back to the attacker
dKey: exports saved passwords from the keychain
dTask: creates a task that runs a payload at every logon
dShadow: deletes the volume shadow copies before encryption
dDl: downloads a tool into a writable folder
capRan0: On {{host}}{{user}}, a process starts touching hundreds of files at once.
capRan1: Files get renamed with {{exts}}: the data is being encrypted in place.
capRan2: A ransom note is written: the attacker asks for payment to restore the data.
capRan2b: Backups and shadow copies are deleted: no easy way back.
capRan3: Restore from offline backups and find the entry point before the encryption spreads.
capPer0: On {{host}}{{user}}, something writes to system startup locations.
capPer1: It drops {{what}}: these run automatically on every boot or logon.
capPer2: Last piece in place: {{what}}. The foothold now survives reboots.
capPer3: Remove the persistence artifacts and hunt for the initial infection vector.
dPersistCron: runs the payload on a schedule
dPersistLaunch: launches the payload when the user logs in
dPersistKey: lets the attacker SSH back in
dPersistRc: runs the payload in every new shell
dPersistPs: runs the payload in every PowerShell session
capExf0: On {{host}}{{user}}, sensitive data is staged into one archive.
capExf2: The data arrives at {{dest}}: it is now outside the company.
capExf3: Block the transfer, revoke access to {{dest}} and find who can reach that data.
capEv0: On {{host}}, the attacker starts reaching for the things that watch it.
capEv1: {{what}} is turned off: one fewer thing that can see them.
capEv2: The logs are wiped: the trail of what they did is gone.
capEv2b: With {{what}} disabled, the host is now blind to the attacker.
capEv3: Restore the disabled tools and preserve the remaining logs before they go too.
capPe0: On {{host}}, the session runs as a normal user.{{user}}
capPe1: It uses {{method}} to reach a higher privilege level.
capPe2: The commands now run as {{account}}: full control of the host.
capPe3: Terminate the escalated session and audit what {{account}} was able to touch.
capUe0: On {{host}}{{user}}, the user downloads a file and opens it.
capUe1: The file is opened: {{file}} is trusted and executed.
capUe2: {{app}} starts a child process that runs {{payload}}.
capUe3: Quarantine the file, block its hash and check for other machines that opened it.
capSd0: {{src}} pushes software toward {{to}} over the network.
capSd1: It uses {{tool}}: a channel that installs without user interaction.
capSd2: The package is installed on {{to}} and starts with it.
capSd3: Stop the deployment, remove the installed component and audit what it did.
capPh0: {{name}} sends a phishing email into the company.
capPh1: The message lands in {{user}}'s inbox and is opened.
capPh2: The attachment runs: {{file}} executes on the machine.
capPh3: Quarantine the email, block the sender and remove {{file}} from {{user}}'s machine.
capPi1: It injects code into a trusted process: {{victim}}.
capPi2: {{victim}} now runs the attacker's code with its own privileges.
capPi3: Kill the injected code, remove the loader and check for other injection victims.
capCd0: On {{host}}, a tool starts reading the credential store.
capCd1: It opens {{store}} and extracts the stored material.
capCd2: {{n}} credentials are captured: accounts, keys and hashes.
capCd3: Rotate every credential in the store and hunt for the dumper tool.
capDd0: On {{host}}, something starts erasing data instead of encrypting it.
capDd1: {{n}} datasets are destroyed, one after another.
capDd2: The data is deleted raw: there is no note, no ransom, no way back.
capDd3: Stop the source process and restore what remains from offline backups.
capTd1: It is downloaded into a writable folder: {{folder}}.
capTd2: The file is executed: {{tool}} is now running.
capTd3: Delete the tool, block its hash and check which hosts ran it.
capCt0: {{src}} talks to {{to}} using a normal-looking protocol.
capCt1: The payload is hidden inside {{proto}} traffic.
capCt2: Commands and data cross the boundary unseen, riding {{proto}}.
capCt3: Cut the tunnel, block the endpoint and check what went through it.
capIoc2: {{ioc}} is on the block list: the connection is cut.
capIoc3: Block {{ioc}} at the edge and check what already left the network.
capPd2: The traffic is dropped: the perimeter held.
capPd3: The traffic crosses {{fw}}: the alert is informational.
capPd4: Review the signature and block the source if it keeps coming.
capAc3: Confirm it was planned, or revert the change made by {{who}}.
capKb2: It reuses the ticket on {{services}}: the DC accepts it each time.
capKb3: Reset the krbtgt password and audit the tickets issued in the last 48 h.
capPs0: On {{host}}, a script starts with encoded content.
capPs1: It decodes a command and disables the anti-malware sensor (AMSI).
capPs2: The decoded command executes: this is a payload, not a script.
capPs2a: AMSI is disabled first, then the encoded command runs unseen.
capPs3: Block the hash, hunt for other machines with the same script.
capRs0: On {{host}}, a process opens a socket to the outside.
capRs1: It connects back to {{name}} on port {{port}}: a reverse shell.
capRs2: A prompt appears: the attacker can now type commands on the host.
capRs3: Kill the connection, isolate {{host}} and find what was typed.
capVm0: The guest VM {{guest}} runs a process with host-level access.
capVm1: It tries to cross the hypervisor boundary.
capVm2: The process runs on the {{host}} host: the guest is no longer a cage.
capVm3: Panic the hypervisor, snapshot the guest and rebuild it.
